The same set of people, places, or molecules is often linked in more than one way. Colleagues work
together, ask each other for advice, and are friends; cities are joined by roads, railways, and
flights; genes interact physically, are expressed together, and modify each other's effects. A
network with several kinds of tie among the same nodes is a *multiplex* network, and each kind of
tie forms one of its *layers*.

Analyzing the layers separately misses how they combine, and merging them into a single network
loses the differences between them. EdgeCase supports both views and the steps in between. A single
graph can hold every layer at once, with the edge `rel` naming each edge's layer, and the
[`MultiplexGraph`](../reference/MultiplexGraph.qmd) class holds the layers as separate graphs on a
shared set of nodes, with methods that analyze them together. This page builds a small multiplex
network and shows both.

## A multiplex network

Consider a small consultancy of twelve people in two teams, strategy and data, whose ties were
recorded in a staff survey. The example is constructed for this page. Three kinds of tie were
asked about: who worked on a project together in the past year, who are friends, and who regularly
discuss work problems and ask each other for advice. The ties are recorded as mutual, so all three
layers are undirected:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

staff = {
    "Ana": "strategy", "Ben": "strategy", "Cara": "strategy",
    "Dev": "strategy", "Eli": "strategy", "Fay": "strategy",
    "Gus": "data", "Hana": "data", "Ivo": "data",
    "Jun": "data", "Kai": "data", "Lea": "data",
}

ties = {
    "project": [
        ("Ana", "Ben"), ("Ana", "Cara"), ("Ben", "Cara"), ("Cara", "Dev"), ("Dev", "Eli"),
        ("Eli", "Fay"), ("Dev", "Fay"), ("Ben", "Dev"), ("Gus", "Hana"), ("Gus", "Ivo"),
        ("Hana", "Ivo"), ("Ivo", "Jun"), ("Jun", "Kai"), ("Kai", "Lea"), ("Jun", "Lea"),
        ("Hana", "Jun"), ("Cara", "Hana"), ("Dev", "Ivo"),
    ],
    "friendship": [
        ("Ben", "Cara"), ("Eli", "Fay"), ("Eli", "Kai"), ("Fay", "Kai"), ("Fay", "Lea"),
        ("Kai", "Lea"), ("Jun", "Kai"), ("Ben", "Jun"), ("Hana", "Ivo"), ("Ana", "Gus"),
        ("Dev", "Eli"),
    ],
    "advice": [
        ("Ana", "Ben"), ("Ana", "Cara"), ("Ana", "Dev"), ("Ana", "Eli"), ("Ana", "Fay"),
        ("Gus", "Hana"), ("Gus", "Ivo"), ("Gus", "Jun"), ("Gus", "Kai"), ("Gus", "Lea"),
        ("Ana", "Gus"), ("Hana", "Cara"), ("Hana", "Dev"), ("Hana", "Ben"),
    ],
}
```

Ana leads the strategy team and Gus the data team, and Hana is the data team's most experienced
analyst. The two representations are built from these dictionaries in turn.

## One graph with typed edges

The simplest representation is a single graph in which every tie is an edge, and the edge's `rel`
records the layer it belongs to. [`add_edges()`](../reference/Graph.add_edges.qmd) sets the `rel`
of a whole batch at once. Two people linked in several layers get several parallel edges, one per
layer, which EdgeCase allows in any graph:

```{python}
office = ec.Graph(graph_name="office")
for name, team in staff.items():
    office.add_node(name, team=team)
for layer, edges in ties.items():
    office.add_edges(edges, rel=layer)

office.count_nodes(), office.count_edges()
```

The 43 edges are the 18 project ties, 11 friendships, and 14 advice ties. The edge table shows the
layer of each edge in its `rel` column, so a layer is a filter on that column, and the methods that
accept a `rel` filter, as well as Cypher queries, can read one layer or combine several (see
[Node and edge data](07-node-and-edge-data.qmd#types-and-relationship-types)):

```{python}
office.get_edge_df().group_by("rel", maintain_order=True).len()
```

Cypher patterns name relationship types directly, which makes questions across layers easy to ask.
The pairs who work together and are also friends:

```{python}
office.match(
    "MATCH (a)-[:project]-(b), (a)-[:friendship]-(b) WHERE a.name < b.name RETURN a.name, b.name"
)
```

Six of the eighteen project partnerships are also friendships. The condition `a.name < b.name`
keeps one row per pair, since an undirected pattern matches each pair in both directions.
[Cypher queries](10-cypher.qmd) describes the query language.

### Describing the layers together

Multiplex networks have measures of their own, which describe how the layers relate. All of them
can be computed from the edge table with Polars, once the endpoints are given as labels. The
*multiplexity* of a pair is the number of layers in which the two are linked. Writing each pair
with its two names in alphabetical order lets `group_by()` collect the layers of each pair:

```{python}
label_of = dict(office.get_node_df().select("id", "label").iter_rows())
edges = office.get_edge_df().with_columns(
    pl.col("source", "target").replace_strict(label_of, return_dtype=pl.String)
)
pairs = (
    edges.with_columns(
        a=pl.min_horizontal("source", "target"), b=pl.max_horizontal("source", "target")
    )
    .group_by("a", "b")
    .agg(pl.col("rel").sort().alias("layers"), pl.len().alias("multiplexity"))
    .sort("multiplexity", "a", "b", descending=[True, False, False])
)
pairs
```

The 43 ties link 31 different pairs. Twelve pairs are linked in two layers and none in all three,
and the combinations show how the layers relate: work and friendship overlap among peers, such as
Ben and Cara, while work and advice overlap where a leader works with a team member, such as Ana and
Ben. The overlap between two layers can be measured directly with the Jaccard index of their sets
of pairs, the share of the pairs linked in either layer that are linked in both:

```{python}
from itertools import combinations


def pair_set(layer):
    rows = edges.filter(pl.col("rel") == layer).select(
        a=pl.min_horizontal("source", "target"), b=pl.max_horizontal("source", "target")
    )
    return set(rows.iter_rows())


layer_pairs = {layer: pair_set(layer) for layer in ties}
{
    (x, y): round(len(layer_pairs[x] & layer_pairs[y]) / len(layer_pairs[x] | layer_pairs[y]), 3)
    for x, y in combinations(ties, 2)
}
```

Project work overlaps most with friendship and somewhat with advice, while friendship and advice
share only a single pair, Ana and Gus. In this office, people ask advice of the team leaders and
of Hana rather than of their friends.

### Degrees by layer

A node's degree can be counted in each layer separately. `pivot()` turns the endpoints of the edges
into a table of degrees, with one row per person and one column per layer:

```{python}
ends = pl.concat(
    [edges.select(node="source", layer="rel"), edges.select(node="target", layer="rel")]
)
degrees = (
    ends.pivot(on="layer", index="node", values="layer", aggregate_function="len")
    .fill_null(0)
    .sort("node")
)
degrees
```

The table shows different roles at a glance. Ana and Gus have most of their ties in the advice
layer, Kai's are mostly friendships, and Dev is the busiest collaborator. The *participation
coefficient* summarizes how evenly a node's ties are spread over the layers. For *M* layers, it is
*M* / (*M* − 1) times one minus the sum of the squared shares of the node's ties in each layer, so
it is 0 for a node whose ties are all in one layer and 1 for a node whose ties are spread evenly
over all of them:

```{python}
n_layers = len(ties)
(
    ends.group_by("node", "layer")
    .len()
    .with_columns(share=pl.col("len") / pl.col("len").sum().over("node"))
    .group_by("node")
    .agg(
        ties=pl.col("len").sum(),
        participation=n_layers / (n_layers - 1) * (1 - (pl.col("share") ** 2).sum()),
    )
    .sort("participation", descending=True)
)
```

Ben, with three project ties, two friendships, and two advice ties, takes part most evenly in all
three layers. The two team leaders have the lowest participation, since their roles concentrate
their ties in a single layer. Measures like this distinguish people whom a single aggregated
network would treat alike: Ana, Gus, and Hana all have nine ties, but of very different kinds.

### Drawing the layers

Layers are easiest to compare when they are drawn with the same positions for the nodes, so that
each picture shows a different set of edges on the same map. A layout computed once for the whole
office, stored in the `pos` attribute, can be given to every layer (see [Layouts](23-layouts.qmd)).
The layers themselves are built as separate graphs, each with all twelve people:

```{python}
office.layout_spring(seed=3)
positions = dict(office.get_node_df().select("label", "pos").iter_rows())


def build_layer(edges):
    layer = ec.Graph()
    for name, team in staff.items():
        layer.add_node(name, team=team)
    layer.add_edges(edges)
    layer.set_node_attrs("pos", positions)
    return layer


layers = {name: build_layer(edges) for name, edges in ties.items()}
layers["project"].plot(
    layout="pos", color_by="team", palette="Set2", label_by="label", node_size=11, height=340
)
```

The project layer shows the two teams, each a dense cluster, linked by the two cross-team projects
of Cara and Hana and of Dev and Ivo. The friendship layer, drawn on the same map, cuts across the
teams:

```{python}
layers["friendship"].plot(
    layout="pos", color_by="team", palette="Set2", label_by="label", node_size=11, height=340
)
```

Five of the eleven friendships link the two teams: three within a group of friends around Kai, Fay,
Eli, and Lea, one between Ben and Jun, and one between the two leaders, Ana and Gus. The advice
layer, finally, is a pair of stars, centered on Ana and Gus, with Hana as a third source of advice
for the strategy team:

```{python}
layers["advice"].plot(
    layout="pos", color_by="team", palette="Set2", label_by="label", node_size=11, height=340
)
```

## The MultiplexGraph class

[`MultiplexGraph`](../reference/MultiplexGraph.qmd) holds a set of layers as separate `Graph`
objects, keyed by layer name, and provides methods that analyze all of them at once. Every layer
must contain exactly the same node labels, which is why each layer above has all twelve people,
including those without ties in that layer. The layer graphs keep their own node and edge
attributes:

```{python}
office_mpx = ec.MultiplexGraph(layers)
office_mpx
```

`layer_names` lists the layers, `layers` returns the dictionary of layer graphs, `get_layer()`
returns one layer by name, and `count_nodes()`, `count_layers()`, and `node_labels()` describe the
shared nodes. Each layer is an ordinary graph, so every EdgeCase method works on it:

```{python}
office_mpx.get_layer("advice").pagerank(return_dict=True)[1]
```

The scores are keyed by node ID, and Ana is node 1. Her PageRank in the advice layer alone is
about 0.2, more than twice the average of 1/12. Building a
`MultiplexGraph` from layers whose node labels differ raises a `ValueError`, which catches layers
built from inconsistent data before any analysis runs. A node that is missing from a layer should be
added to it as an isolated node.

### PageRank across layers

`multiplex_pagerank()` ranks the nodes by all
the layers together. It adds the layers into a single weighted network, in which each tie counts
with its own weight (1 if it has none) times the weight of its layer, and runs PageRank on the
result. With `return_dict=True`, it returns the scores keyed by node label:

```{python}
combined = office_mpx.multiplex_pagerank(return_dict=True)
sorted(combined.items(), key=lambda item: -item[1])[:4]
```

With all layers weighted equally, Gus, Ana, and Hana are almost tied at the top, each with nine
ties in total, while Dev, the busiest collaborator, comes fourth. `layer_weights=` sets how much
each layer counts, which turns the ranking into an answer to a specific question. Who matters most
for getting work done, counting advice twice and ignoring friendship?

```{python}
work = office_mpx.multiplex_pagerank(
    layer_weights={"project": 1.0, "friendship": 0.0, "advice": 2.0}, return_dict=True
)
sorted(work.items(), key=lambda item: -item[1])[:4]
```

The three sources of advice now pull clearly ahead, with scores between 0.12 and 0.15 against 0.095
for Dev, since the advice ties that lead to them count twice and the friendships that spread the
scores across the office don't count at all. A layer omitted from `layer_weights=` counts with
weight 1. `damping=`, `max_iter=`, and `tol=` work as in
[`pagerank()`](../reference/Graph.pagerank.qmd).

### Communities across layers

`multiplex_community_detection()`
finds communities in the same weighted sum of the layers, with the Louvain method by default or
Walktrap with `method="walktrap"`. The results are keyed by node label, so they can be stored on any
of the layers, or on the office graph, with `set_node_attrs()`:

```{python}
groups = office_mpx.multiplex_community_detection(return_dict=True)
office.set_node_attrs("multiplex_cmty", groups)
office.get_node_df().group_by("multiplex_cmty").agg(pl.col("label")).sort("multiplex_cmty")
```

With every layer counted, the communities follow the teams, and each team splits into two working
groups. Weighting the layers differently finds different structure. Counting only friendship, the
communities are circles of friends instead, and the friends around Kai, Fay, Eli, and Lea form a
community that spans both teams:

```{python}
friends = office_mpx.multiplex_community_detection(
    layer_weights={"project": 0.0, "friendship": 1.0, "advice": 0.0}, return_dict=True
)
office.set_node_attrs("friend_cmty", friends)
office.get_node_df().group_by("friend_cmty").agg(pl.col("label")).sort("friend_cmty")
```

`resolution=` controls the size of the Louvain communities, as in
[`cmty_louvain()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_louvain.qmd), with higher values giving more and smaller
communities. [Community detection](14-communities.qmd) describes both methods.

## Flattening layers yourself

Both `MultiplexGraph` methods work on the weighted sum of the layers. Building that sum directly,
as an ordinary weighted graph, opens the rest of EdgeCase to the combined network. The multiplexity
table computed above already has one row per pair and the number of layers linking it, which
becomes the weight:

```{python}
flat = ec.from_pandas_edgelist(
    pairs.rename({"multiplexity": "weight"}), source="a", target="b", edge_attr="weight"
)
flat.count_nodes(), flat.count_edges(), flat.is_weighted()
```

The 31 pairs become 31 weighted edges, and any method that reads weights as tie strengths, such
as [`pagerank()`](../reference/Graph.pagerank.qmd) or the community detection methods, now treats a
tie that spans two layers as twice as strong. For methods that read weights as distances, such as
the shortest paths and betweenness, a stronger tie should be a shorter one, so the weight is better
inverted first, as described in [Paths and distances](12-paths.qmd). A weighted sum with other
layer weights is a `group_by()` on the edge table with a weight looked up for each `rel`.

Flattening is also the route for large networks. The `MultiplexGraph` methods are implemented in
Python, and suit networks of up to a few hundred nodes, while the flattened graph can use the Rust
implementations of every EdgeCase method, at any size.

## Summary

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| Hold all layers in one graph | one edge per tie, with `rel` naming the layer, via `add_edges(rel=)` |
| Query across layers | Cypher patterns with relationship types, such as `[:project]` and `[:friendship]` |
| Multiplexity and layer overlap | `group_by()` on the edge table, with the pairs in a fixed order |
| Degrees and participation by layer | `pivot()` and `group_by()` on the endpoints of the edges |
| Compare layers visually | one layout, stored in `pos` and shared by every layer |
| Hold layers as separate graphs | `MultiplexGraph({name: graph, ...})`, with identical node labels |
| Rank nodes across layers | `multiplex_pagerank(layer_weights=)` |
| Find communities across layers | `multiplex_community_detection(layer_weights=, method=)` |
| Use any method on the combined network | a weighted graph of the pairs, with multiplexity as weight |
